one_line: The final answer is right: a fan is needed, Tj about 94 C (truth 102.3 +-10), Rsa 3.6 K/W, tau 640 s. But for four of six turns the assistant said 'NO fan' (81, 77, 84 C). It changed its answer only after the person found the catalogue's dT=75 K footnote himself. The tool plots were SVG paths he could not use.

traps.trap: Single-vertical-plate correlation ignores boundary-layer merging in the 5.25 mm fin gaps (channel h ~3.1 vs plate ~5.7 W/m2K)
Catalogue 3 K/W is rated at dT = 75 K; the real Rsa at the actual ~37 K rise is much higher
Company Tj limit is 90 C, not the 150-175 C silicon limit
Use the real Rjc 1.15 K/W and insulating pad 1.4 K/W, not generic values
Lumped warm-up needs C = m cp and R = Rsa (thermal_transient has no heat input)

trap_notes: Trap 1: from turn 2 on the assistant mentioned in words that narrow channels lower h. It still declared 'NO fan' at 84 C using an h of 9 W/m2K, which it called 'pessimistic' although that h is higher than even the isolated-plate value. Trap 2: the assistant only got this right after the person read the footnote out in turn 5 (the assistant had suggested in turn 2 asking for the catalogue's test conditions). Traps 3 and 4: in turn 1 the assistant invented a 125 C design target and recalled Rjc 1.0 K/W and an interface of 0.5 K/W instead of asking, and the person corrected both.

honesty.issue: Turn 6: 'thermal_convection (flat-plate laminar ...) gives 11.3 W/(m2.K) at 0.2 m/s and 8.0 at 0.1 m/s'. No call at 0.1 m/s was made; the calls were at 0.2 m/s (h 11.27) and 0.5 m/s (h 17.82). The 8.0 is the assistant's own scaling, presented as tool output.
Turn 1: Rjc '1.0 K/W (the typical datasheet maximum for the IRF540N)' was recalled from memory and is wrong (datasheet 1.15 K/W). It was listed under assumptions but worded as a datasheet fact.

Turns 3-4: the answer was given as a firm 'NO fan, 84 C', with h = 9 W/m2K called 'pessimistic'. That h was the assistant's own judgement, and it is optimistic. In turn 4 the assistant admitted that the 2.3 K/W is 'judgement, not data', but by then the person had already written '84C with the fan not needed, fine'.

Good: the placeholder 0.1 m2 area and the ambient trick in thermal_transient were disclosed ('only the product hA = 1/3 W/K affects the result'). Sums done by hand were marked 'my arithmetic on the tool's resistances'.

problems.what: thermal_convection has no correlation for natural convection in fin arrays or parallel-plate channels (Elenbaas / Bar-Cohen-Rohsenow). For any finned heatsink with gaps under about 10 mm, the only option is the isolated-plate value, which is about 1.8x too high here. That is why turns 2-4 gave Rsa 1.5-2.3 K/W and a 'no fan' verdict.
problems.evidence: In-process: thermal_convection natural_vertical_plate, length 100 mm, Ts 82 degC, Tinf 45 degC, air k 0.0285 rho 1.05 mu 1.95e-5 cp 1007 -> h = 5.78 W/m2K (Ra 2.15e6). Truth channel correlation for the 5.25 mm gap: h = 3.12 W/m2K.
problems.fix: Add correlation 'natural_vertical_channel' (Bar-Cohen/Rohsenow isothermal parallel plates: inputs gap s, length L along the flow; Nu_s = [576/(Ra*)^2 + 2.873/(Ra*)^0.5]^-0.5 with Ra* = Ra_s s/L), plus a warning on natural_vertical_plate: 'for fin arrays with gap < ~10 mm the boundary layers merge; use natural_vertical_channel'.

problems.what: The thermal_convection 'length' description ('plate length / height') is ambiguous for heatsinks. The assistant took the 24 mm fin height as the plate length, even after the person said the fins run vertically along 100 mm with air rising between them. Over that 4x shorter length h comes out 42 % higher.
problems.evidence: Turn 3 input: {correlation: natural_vertical_plate, length: '24 mm', ... surface 57 degC}. In-process at the same conditions (Ts 82 C): L=24 mm -> h 8.19, L=100 mm -> h 5.78 W/m2K.
problems.fix: eng_toolkit/domains/thermal/convection.py, 'length' Field: add 'natural_vertical_*: the vertical extent the air rises along (for an upright heatsink, the fin length in the flow direction, not the fin height off the base)'.

problems.what: The assistant gave a confident wrong verdict ('no fan') for four turns. Turn 1 invented a 125 C target and recalled Rjc 1.0 / interface 0.5 instead of asking. Turns 3-4 called an assumed total h of 9 W/m2K a 'pessimistic' design number. The verdict flipped only when the person brought up the dT=75 K footnote.
problems.evidence: Turn 1: 'no fan is needed on this estimate. The junction is about 81 C'. Turn 3: 'Answer: NO fan. Estimated junction temperature is about 84 C'. Turn 5: 'Yes, a fan is needed ... My earlier 84 C was too optimistic'.
problems.fix: Add a thermal / heatsink workflow skill (plugin/skills/eng-thermal-check). It should: ask for the user's Tj limit, Rjc and interface from the datasheet; ask for the conditions behind a catalogue Rth (dT, orientation, length); for closely spaced fins call the result optimistic and the verdict borderline unless a channel correlation is used; never call an assumed h 'pessimistic' without a bound.

problems.what: thermal_transient 'lumped' has no heat-input term and returns one temperature per call. To draw a warm-up curve the assistant set ambient = steady temperature and h*A = 1/Rsa on a placeholder 0.1 m2 area, then called the tool 8-10 times per curve, about 45 calls in total over 5 curves.
problems.evidence: e.g. turn 6: thermal_transient {model lumped, initial 45 degC, ambient_temperature '73.8 degC', surface_area '0.1 m^2', h '2.7778 W/(m^2*K)', time '60 s'} repeated for 150, 300, ... 3600 s.
problems.fix: thermal_transient lumped: add 'heat_input' (W) [dT/dt = (P - hA(T - Tinf))/(rho V cp)], optional 'thermal_resistance' instead of h*A, and a 'times' list or t_final/points that writes transient.csv (time_s, temperature) for plot_xy.

problems.what: plot_xy only produces SVG. In this client the person cannot see it or paste it into a slide. The assistant spent parts of three turns on workarounds: tool checks in Bash and PowerShell, a matplotlib script it could not run, a .NET drawing script that was blocked, and finally a canvas chart in HTML it wrote by hand with a Download PNG button.
problems.evidence: Person turn 2: 'The plot is just an svg path, I need something I can paste into a slide.' Turn 4: 'I still have no png ... can you just make the png yourself'.
problems.fix: plot_xy / plot_panels / plot_bar: add format='png' (and 'pdf'), rendered server-side (matplotlib or resvg) at a slide-friendly size. Change eng-plot-results SKILL.md 'Not covered: ... PNG/PDF' accordingly.

problems.what: plot_xy's automatic x range pads below zero for data that start at 0, so a time axis runs from -500 s.
problems.evidence: Run job 20261026T041425Z-4d0976b5-plot_xy: series x [0 ... 3600], no x_range -> data.panels[0].axes.x.min = -500.0, ticks start at '-500'. Reproduced in-process with the same series (ok, auto range).
problems.fix: In the automatic range, do not extend past 0 when the data minimum is >= 0 (the same for the maximum when it is <= 0); snap nice-number padding to the data's sign.

problems.what: In turn 6 an h value at 0.1 m/s was quoted as a thermal_convection result although that call was never made. The fan estimate also mixes an uncalibrated flat-plate forced h with the natural case, which had been scaled down by 2.4.
problems.evidence: Text: 'thermal_convection ... gives 11.3 W/(m2.K) at 0.2 m/s and 8.0 at 0.1 m/s'. Calls: velocity '0.2 m/s' -> h 11.27; velocity '0.5 m/s' -> h 17.82.
problems.fix: eng-toolkit SKILL.md rule 6/7: 'Attribute to a tool only numbers that a call returned; mark derived or scaled numbers as yours.'

problems.what: There are three smaller inconsistencies. The fin gap is given as 4.7 mm (60-18)/9; it is (60-18)/8 = 5.25 mm. The calibrated Rsa was evaluated at the person's '~20 K' rise, although the assistant's own result (3.6 K/W x 8 W) is a 28.8 K rise. The thermal_conduction tool was used as an adder for series resistances ('1 m @ 1 W/(m*K)' layers).
problems.evidence: Turn 3 'Fin gaps are about 4.7 mm'. Turn 5 'At 20 K, the same model gives Rsa 1.49 K/W ... Rsa ~ 3.6 K/W'. Turn 1 thermal_conduction layers '1 m @ 1 W/(m*K); 0.5 m @ 1 W/(m*K); 3 m @ 1 W/(m*K)'.
problems.fix: eng-toolkit SKILL.md: allow simple sums and products of tool outputs when they are labelled as the assistant's own (the current 'never do the arithmetic yourself' pushes it to misuse tools as calculators). Make the skill ask for iteration when a property depends on the result (h(dT)).

problems.what: The assistant had Bash, PowerShell and Write tools (the brief says only mcp__eng-toolkit__*, Skill and Read). Running Python and .NET was denied, so it wrote files into a different session's scratchpad and pointed the person there. The person also produced the key footnote in turn 5. That is plausible because the assistant had suggested checking the test conditions, but it is the persona's facts that saved the answer.
problems.evidence: Turn 2 tools: Bash x4, PowerShell x2, Write make_slide_png.py; 'I did not run it, because running Python needs an approval I haven't been given.'
problems.fix: In the harness, restrict allowed_tools to the stated set, or allow the scratch writes explicitly, so the runs measure the toolkit.

what_worked: The Tj chain was rebuilt correctly when the person gave the real values: 1.15 + 1.40 + 3.0 K/W -> Tj 89.4 C, and Rsa <= 3.07 K/W is needed for 90 C (both match truth).
Mass check from geometry: '73 cm3 ... 198 g, which matches your mass' (truth 198 g).
Once the dT=75 K footnote was known, the assistant calibrated to the catalogue and gave an honest range (94-99 C, 'None of them passes 90 C'), and the verdict came out right.
The thermal_transient time constant and values were checked against the analytic form (T = 69 - 24 e^(-t/540) at 540 s: 60.17 C).
Limits were stated: closed-box air heating, fan recirculation without a vent, and a measurement procedure with two thermocouples.
